items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I learned all the songs. And I said now that, that’s music. That’s something I can do.

ctx.x: Wow. Did use of your vocal thing come along naturally. I know I’ve been reading about Nat King Cole who — it was suggested to him like, you need to start singing, or could you, and from there, it’s history.

Well I played in I think it was the beginning of college. Since I was already singing and playing in rock bands through high school, when I went to college I had my guitar and I had with me the Kenny Rankin album, I had some Michael Franks records, and some James Taylor stuff. And I had seen guys who sat and played the guitar, you know, folk guys. And so I learned some of these Kenny Rankin songs, like “Haven’t We Met” and he did “Here’s that Rainy Day,” and he did “Sunny Gets Blue” on this one record. And then I…

minutes and he’d say “sing, sing something.” And he’d say — and I’d do “Straighten Up and Fly Right,” “For Sentimental Reasons.” And then we would close out. We would do an Ellington medley and “Sing Sing Sing” or a little Goodman medley. And so as luck would have it, it’s amazing, it’s weird thinking about it because it’s so long ago to me now. In 1983, in May of ’83 I was singing this tune “I Like Jersey Best.” A buddy of mine wrote this song about our state, make a little rock & roll record with my friend…

items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And then there’s the Joe Mooney records and then the Nat Cole records. So but I mean I was never really outside of that circle.

ctx.x: I know who you’re talking about. At least two or three people, yes.

And so you know that kind of thing, but I mean the good news is is there’s a lot of great music out there. There’s a lot of kids who now can learn in high school and in college from real live great teachers of jazz. I mean a guy like Isaiah, they — you know Isaiah and Mike, and Mike’s a product of the New School I think, too. And Isaiah out of Juilliard. And they’ll sit and they’ll sing choruses on these records they listen to. I make it sound like these records they listen to — but they’re so immersed in it. And…

mentioned that Sebesky record a number of times in other interviews I was looking at today. And Sebesky was a big part of my life in the ‘90s and well just from the ‘90s all the way ‘til his passing. You know somebody like Don Sebesky, you know, writing these arrangements and then you start to see how he harmonizes stuff and you go oh yeah that was cool. So when you start to write the chords out for somebody you go what would Don have done here? You know that was a gift.
